title: GOTCHA: scraper vs raw DOM tree - index-based traversal
description:
The TS version uses raw DOM tree walking with indices (children[n]).
The Rust scraper library uses Selector + iterators, not indices.

SOLUTION: domStroll manually filters & indexes children, then accesses by position.
This works but may need tweaking if website HTML structure has unexpected text nodes.

TEST: Validate that domStroll handles text nodes correctly (should skip or error as needed).

title: GOTCHA: Website structure changes - validation needed
description:
Dictionary websites update their HTML structure frequently.
The TS version already has TODO comments about this (e.g., oxfordlearners TODO).

MITIGATION:
- Test each checker against LIVE websites before marking done
- Keep debug flag enabled during testing to see actual structure
- Document expected structure in comments
- Add error messages that guide troubleshooting

title: INVESTIGATE: Can we use smol + reqwest with default-features=false?
description:
User found that reqwest CAN work with smol if:
1. Disable default-features on reqwest 
2. Use rustls-tls instead of tokio
3. Add hickory-dns for async DNS

Current setup: tokio (heavier than needed for CLI tool)
Goal: Verify if smol actually works and is lighter

Test approach:
- Create branch with smol config
- Try the example from research
- Benchmark binary size & startup time if it works
- Decide: keep smol if benefits outweigh complexity, else keep tokio
notes:
TESTED: The research was partially correct but smol doesn't work with reqwest in practice.

Why it failed:
- reqwest 0.12 + disable default-features + rustls-tls: still pulls in tokio
- hickory-dns itself depends on tokio (via hickory-resolver, etc)
- hyper 1.x inside reqwest needs tokio for its reactor
- Fundamental issue: hyper's DNS resolver is tokio-dependent

Result: Even disabling default-features, tokio is still a transitive dependency via hyper->tokio.

Decision: KEEP TOKIO. It's fine for a CLI tool (small startup overhead, good ecosystem support).
The added complexity of forcing smol isn't worth the marginal savings.

title: Phase 5: Helper functions & main logic (etymonline, etym, integration)
description:
Implement helper functions and integrate everything:

- etym(): Complex etymonline.com scraper with substring matching
- etymonline(): Wrapper calling etym() with result[0] only
- Main checker_all(): Parallel execution of all 13 checkers
- Result aggregation: pros vs community dicts
- Output formatting with branching logic
- Integration tests against live sites

title: Phase 4: Complex DOM checkers (ahd, mw, oxfordlearners, wordnet, wordnik)
description:
Implement complex DOM structure checkers:

- ahd: div#results children count & type patterns
- mw: body class check, then deep dive for partial matches
- oxfordlearners: 10+ level deep DOM traversal with multiple validates
- wordnet: tag sequence validation (form, form, h3)
- wordnik: guts.active structure with alternating h3/ul pattern

These need deep domStroll paths (5-10+ steps).

title: GOTCHA: reqwest/tokio forced us to switch from smol
description:
Initial plan was to use smol (lightweight, single-threaded).
Problem: reqwest depends on tokio by default, and hyper (its HTTP layer) requires a tokio runtime.
Solution: Switched to tokio with rt-multi-thread feature.

DECISION: tokio is fine for a CLI tool. If startup time becomes issue, can revisit.
Keep code runtime-agnostic in lib.rs (only main.rs knows about tokio).

title: Phase 3: Redirect & simple DOM checkers (cambridge, chambers, dictcom, longman)
description:
Implement redirect and simple DOM structure checkers:

- cambridge: check_redirect() returns true if NOT redirect
- chambers: DOM p.message child count (1 = found, 3 = not found)
- dictcom: main element children.length (3 = not found, 4 = found)
- longman: head.metadata class presence

These use domStroll with shallow paths (2-5 steps).

title: Phase 2: API-based checkers (urban, oed, wikt)
description:
Implement Urban Dictionary, Oxford English Dict, and Wiktionary checkers

These are simple JSON API checkers:
- urban: list.length check
- oed: array.some() with element matching
- wikt: Wiktionary API with language parameter

All return Option<bool> or null on error.
